title: BOD: measuring pollution by the oxygen microbes use

Why is the BOD test five days?

stages.ask: Why is BOD measured over 5 days?

explain.say: Why five days? A British Royal Commission on sewage, early in the twentieth century, picked five days at twenty degrees Celsius, the story goes, because no British river takes longer to reach the sea. The test they set up, BOD, is still the world's favourite measure of how dirty water is. Let us see how it is done.

explain.say: Follow the chain. BOD, biochemical oxygen demand, is the oxygen microbes use while eating the dirt. We dilute six millilitres of sewage into a three hundred millilitre bottle, a fraction of zero point zero two. Oxygen falls from eight point six to four point five in five dark days. So BOD five is four point one over zero point zero two: two hundred and five milligrams per litre.

explain.say: Now the curve. The microbes eat fast at first, then slow down as food runs out. Total demand, called ultimate BOD, here is three hundred milligrams per litre. With a rate of zero point two three per day, about sixty eight percent is used by day five: that is our two hundred and five. By day twenty it is nearly all gone. What share would be used by day ten, more or less than ninety percent?

marks.label: BOD₅ = 205 mg/L
marks.ask: Why is BOD measured over 5 days?

explain.say: Just under ninety! Here is why BOD matters. Pour waste into a river and microbes downstream use up its oxygen. See the sag: oxygen drops from eight to its lowest, three point seven milligrams per litre, after about two point eight days of flow, then the river breathes in air and recovers. Many fish struggle below about five.

explain.say: Engineers use this sag curve to set how clean a discharge must be, so the lowest point stays safe for fish. COD, chemical oxygen demand, is a faster test using a strong chemical, done in a couple of hours. Great work! Challenge: if the ultimate BOD were one hundred, about what would BOD five be?

faq.a: Biochemical oxygen demand is the amount of dissolved oxygen microbes use while breaking down the organic matter in water, usually measured over 5 days at 20 degrees Celsius. Raw sewage is often 200 to 400 milligrams per litre.

faq.q: Why is BOD measured over 5 days?
faq.a: The 5-day, 20 degree test was set by the British Royal Commission on Sewage Disposal in the early 1900s. By day 5 most of the easily eaten matter, about two thirds, has been used.
Ultimate BOD, L0, is the total oxygen the microbes would use given unlimited time. BOD at time t is L0 times 1 minus e to the minus k t; with k of 0.23 per day, BOD5 is about 68 percent of L0.

faq.q: What is the oxygen sag curve?
faq.a: It shows dissolved oxygen in a river below a waste outfall: oxygen falls as microbes eat, reaches a lowest point, then recovers as air dissolves back in. The Streeter–Phelps equation predicts it.

faq.q: What is the difference between BOD and COD?
faq.a: BOD measures oxygen used by microbes over 5 days. COD uses a strong chemical oxidant to oxidise almost everything in about 2 hours, so COD is always higher than BOD.

facts: The standard BOD test runs for 5 days at 20 °C in the dark.
H. W. Streeter and Earle Phelps published their oxygen sag model for the Ohio River in 1925.
